executive_summary:
Samples healthverity operates at the intersection of real-world healthcare data and commercial opportunity, where the ability to translate claims, cohorts, and provider networks into trusted, licensable products defines competitive advantage. The use cases in this catalog position the organization to convert its vast patient and claims assets into revenue-generating offerings with the precision and speed the market now demands.

Concrete impact is already within reach. Reveal Emerging Condition Trends to Grow Revenue lets commercial teams refresh and promote rising-condition cohorts ahead of demand, while Segment Patient Utilization to Grow Revenue sharpens which cohorts to package and license. On the integrity side, Detect Billing Anomalies to Prevent Revenue Loss protects the value of the underlying data by surfacing a ranked provider investigation queue before quality issues reach customers.

Databricks Genie Code is the accelerant for this transformation, enabling analysts, curators, and partnership leads to interrogate complex healthcare data in natural language and move from question to insight without friction. For Samples healthverity, this means faster dataset launches, tighter data quality, and smarter sourcing decisions, all compounding into durable revenue growth.

domains.summary:
The Commercial domain is where Samples healthverity turns healthcare data assets into monetizable products, aligning dataset roadmaps and pricing with genuine market demand. Its core responsibility is to ensure that the right cohorts reach the right buyers at the right moment, maximizing licensing revenue while keeping offerings fresh and defensible.

Several opportunities make this tangible. Reveal Emerging Condition Trends to Grow Revenue allows the Commercial Data Product Manager to prioritize refreshing and promoting rising-condition cohorts, increasing timely licensing. Anticipate Specialty Demand to Grow Revenue helps the Product Roadmap Owner sequence specialty dataset builds against forecast demand, lifting the count of datasets launched into receptive markets. Quantify Cohort Longevity to Grow Revenue equips the Pricing Analyst with observation-window survival estimates to set longitudinal pricing tiers.

With Databricks Genie Code, these teams can explore demand signals and cohort characteristics conversationally, compressing the cycle from market insight to launched, priced product and strengthening Samples healthverity's commercial engine.

use_cases.usecase: Reveal Emerging Condition Trends to Grow Revenue
use_cases.Statement: The mix of conditions in the data captured by `diagnosis_code` over `date_service` shifts over time, and without tracking these trends the commercial team misses rising conditions that represent timely cohort-licensing opportunities for life-sciences clients.
use_cases.Solution: Databricks Genie Code tracks diagnosis-code frequency over time, decomposes trend from seasonality to surface rising and declining conditions, and prioritizes which condition datasets to refresh and promote.

Approach: aggregate distinct hvid and claim counts per diagnosis_code per month from date_service, apply STL decomposition and slope estimation to isolate rising versus declining condition trends, then use ai_query to interpret emerging conditions and recommend dataset refresh and promotion priorities.

use_cases.genie_instruction:
## 1. Decision and Owner
This notebook changes which condition cohorts the commercial team prioritizes for dataset refresh and promotion, by surfacing which `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.diagnosis_code` series are rising or declining over `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.date_service`. The Commercial Data Product Manager owns this decision (sponsored by the Chief Commercial Officer); cadence is not assessed, so treat each run as a fresh single-run recompute. The KPI is growth in diagnosis-code frequency over time (direction: a rising trend with a positive, significant slope is better), measured as [ESTIMATE: depends on `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.diagnosis_code`]. The Commercial Data Product Manager receives the ranked list of conditions with their effect sizes and corrected significance.

## 2. Data Plan
The only table is `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic`, used as event facts (one row per claim service line). There is no join path, so this is a single-table read and join coverage is 1.0. The entity key for the finding is `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.diagnosis_code`; the entity for distinct-patient counts is `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.hvid`; the time column is `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.date_service`, parsed from STRING to a date and truncated to a monthly period. This is an unsupervised trend analysis, so there is no outcome label or open-case exclusion. As-of rule: use only rows where the parsed `date_service` is strictly before `ctx["as_of_date"]`. Population filters: keep rows where `diagnosis_code` is non-null and non-empty, `date_service` parses to a valid date, and (optionally recorded as a column, not dropped) `claim_type` is P or I; exclude rows whose parsed date is null.

## 3. Readiness Checks
`row_count`: count rows in `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic` with a non-null `diagnosis_code` and a parseable `date_service` strictly before `ctx["as_of_date"]`; threshold >= 1. `join_coverage`: single table, so return 1.0; threshold >= 0.8. `smallest_group_rows`: group the filtered rows by `diagnosis_code` and return the minimum per-group row count among groups that will be analyzed (the smallest condition series we intend to test); threshold >= 30. `periods`: count the distinct monthly periods derived from `date_service` (truncate to month) across the filtered rows; threshold >= 2.

## 4. Slot Tasks
`measure_readiness(ctx)` reads only `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic`, applies the population filters and the as-of cutoff, and returns the dict `{'row_count', 'join_coverage', 'smallest_group_rows', 'periods'}` exactly as described in Section 3; return 1.0 for `join_coverage`. `build_inputs(ctx)` reads only `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic`, parses `date_service` to a date, enforces the leakage guard by keeping only rows with parsed date strictly before `ctx["as_of_date"]`, applies the population filters, derives a monthly period column, and returns a Spark DataFrame of filtered rows carrying at least `diagnosis_code`, `hvid`, `claim_type`, the parsed date and the monthly period; no row may reference data on or after the as-of date. `analyze(ctx, inputs)` aggregates per `diagnosis_code` per month into distinct `hvid` counts and claim-row counts, builds one monthly time series per condition, applies STL decomposition (statsmodels) and a trend test (slope estimate) per series, and returns a pandas DataFrame with one row per condition and columns: `entity_id` (the `diagnosis_code`), `segment_or_item` (the condition dimension label, for example the diagnosis code plus whether the series is monthly-claim-count based), `value` (the trend effect size, for example the normalized slope versus the prior-period level), `p_value` (the raw p-value of the trend test), and `n` (rows behind that series); Inspire applies the Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Both input and analysis slots use `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic` only.

## 5. Method and Baseline
Use statsmodels STL seasonal decomposition on each per-condition monthly series to separate trend from seasonality, then a slope-based trend test (for example Mann-Kendall or an OLS slope on the trend component) to produce a signed effect size and p-value per condition. The baseline Inspire compares against is the prior period's level for each series. Acceptance in plain words: every reported rising or declining condition must carry an effect size and must remain significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction at fdr_alpha = 0.05; conditions that do not clear corrected significance are reported but flagged as not significant. Handle data risks as follows: missing or sparse months are the reason the readiness gate requires `periods` >= 2 and `smallest_group_rows` >= 30, so restrict STL to series meeting those minima; seasonality is removed by STL before the slope test so recurring monthly patterns are not read as trend; sparse conditions are excluded by the group-size readiness floor; `date_service` is STRING, so parse defensively and drop unparseable dates rather than guessing. No AI function call is added in these slots; Inspire's explanation and summary cells call `ai_query` on the top rows to interpret emerging conditions and suggest refresh and promotion priorities.

## 6. Output Mapping
Map `entity_label` to the `diagnosis_code` (the condition identifier). `value` is the trend effect size (VALUE_TYPE = 'effect size'), expressed as the signed slope of the condition's frequency trend against the prior-period baseline; positive means rising, negative means declining. `segment_or_item` holds the series dimension, for example the diagnosis code with the metric it was measured on (distinct `hvid` per month or claim rows per month). Each row's top reasons are rule-based: the sign and magnitude of the STL trend slope, the corrected significance status, and the direction versus the prior period. Set `data_quality_flag` to something other than ok when a condition series has fewer than the readiness floor of rows, fewer than two periods of data, a high share of unparseable `date_service` values behind it, or a trend that is not significant after correction. Priority tiers and recommended refresh and promotion actions are assigned by Inspire's rule-based writer, not by Genie Code or an LLM.

## 7. Definition of Done
Verify that all four GENIE SLOT functions (`measure_readiness`, `build_inputs`, `analyze`, and the OUTPUT_COLUMNS or VALUE_TYPE mapping) are filled, cite only `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic` and its real columns, and return exactly the contracted keys and columns. Confirm the notebook ran top to bottom in this session with run controls set to Here and then as the tagged job, that the final contract-check cell printed PASSED, and that no Inspire cell was edited, no threshold changed in code, and no job created or deleted. If the readiness gate raises `InspireReadinessStop`, `InspireNoChampion`, or `InspireRejected`, STOP and show the user the plain message the gate printed, do not lower thresholds, fabricate data, drop a check, or switch tables to force a pass.

use_cases.genie_instruction:
## 1. Decision and Owner

This notebook changes which specialty datasets Samples HealthVerity builds ahead of client demand, by forecasting near-term monthly procedure volume per provider taxonomy so the Product Roadmap Owner can sequence dataset builds against projected growth. The decision owner, cadence, KPI and direction were not assessed in the DECISION BLOCK; based on the use case this is a periodic planning decision where a higher count of specialty datasets launched ahead of demand and fewer late-to-market products is better [ESTIMATE: depends on procedure_code]. The ranked forecast output goes to the Product Roadmap Owner, with the Head of Product as sponsor. This execution pattern registers no model: every run refits and forecasts from the data.

## 2. Data Plan

One table is in scope: `samples`.`healthverity`.`claims_sample_synthetic` serves as the event facts table (claim service lines). There is no join: a single table is read, so the join path is trivial and join coverage is 1.0. The series key (entity) is `claims_sample_synthetic.prov_rendering_std_taxonomy` (the NUCC rendering taxonomy that identifies the clinical specialty). The time column is `claims_sample_synthetic.date_service`, which is a STRING and must be parsed to a calendar date, then truncated to the first day of its month. The volume measure is a count of distinct `claims_sample_synthetic.claim_id` per taxonomy per month. This is a forecasting (not supervised) use case, so there is no labeled outcome rule; the as-of rule is that any forecast origin uses only months whose `date_service` falls strictly before that origin. Population filters: keep rows where `claims_sample_synthetic.prov_rendering_std_taxonomy` is non-null and non-empty and where `claims_sample_synthetic.date_service` parses to a valid date; exclude rows that fail either condition from both readiness and series construction.

## 3. Readiness Checks

- `row_count`: count of rows in `samples`.`healthverity`.`claims_sample_synthetic` with a parseable `claims_sample_synthetic.date_service` on or before `ctx["as_of_date"]` and a non-null, non-empty `claims_sample_synthetic.prov_rendering_std_taxonomy`.
- `join_coverage`: set to 1.0, because the use case reads one table and there is no join path.
- `seasonal_cycles`: the number of complete 12-month seasons spanned by the data, computed as the count of distinct months between the earliest and latest parsed `claims_sample_synthetic.date_service` (on or before the as-of date) divided by SEASON_LENGTH (12).
- `staleness_cadences`: the number of monthly cadences between the latest parsed `claims_sample_synthetic.date_service` and `ctx["as_of_date"]`, measured as whole months.
- `missing_period_rate`: across all qualifying taxonomy series, the share of expected monthly periods (from each series' first month through the overall last month) that have zero rows; computed as missing period-cells divided by total expected period-cells.

## 4. Slot Tasks

Slot 3a (`measure_readiness`): reads `samples`.`healthverity`.`claims_sample_synthetic` only. Parse `claims_sample_synthetic.date_service` to a date, filter to on-or-before `ctx["as_of_date"]` with non-empty `claims_sample_synthetic.prov_rendering_std_taxonomy`, then compute and return the dict with keys `row_count`, `join_coverage` (1.0), `seasonal_cycles`, `staleness_cadences`, `missing_period_rate` exactly as described in section 3.

Slot 4 (`build_inputs`): reads `samples`.`healthverity`.`claims_sample_synthetic` only. Set SEASON_LENGTH = 12 (monthly series, annual seasonality) and HORIZON = 12 (one year of near-term demand; adjust only if the decision needs a shorter horizon). Parse `claims_sample_synthetic.date_service` to a date and truncate to month start as `period`; keep only rows with `period` strictly on or before `ctx["as_of_date"]` and non-empty `claims_sample_synthetic.prov_rendering_std_taxonomy`. Group by taxonomy and month, counting distinct `claims_sample_synthetic.claim_id` as `value`. Fill gaps so each series has one row per month from its first observed month through the overall last month (missing months get value 0). The leakage guard: no row with a `period` on or after any forecast origin may enter that origin's history; because `period` is derived only from `date_service` and the filter is strictly before the as-of date, no future month leaks in. Return a Spark DataFrame with columns `entity_id` (the taxonomy string), `period` (DATE, month start), and `value` (numeric count).

Slot 5 (`forecast`): takes the pandas `history` (entity_id, period, value) and `horizon`. For each `entity_id`, sort by `period`, fit a seasonal model (statsmodels ExponentialSmoothing with trend and seasonal_periods = SEASON_LENGTH where history length allows, falling back to a non-seasonal fit for short series), and produce the next `horizon` monthly periods after that series' last period. Refit on the full given history every call; never register per-series models. Clip forecasts at zero (counts cannot be negative). Return a pandas DataFrame with columns `entity_id`, `period` (the horizon future months), and `forecast`.

Slot 8a (output column mapping): keep OUTPUT_COLUMNS from `output_column_map(CTX["family"], {...})` with `entity_label` mapped to the taxonomy, and keep VALUE_TYPE = 'forecast'. Adjust only the listed entries.

## 5. Method and Baseline

Candidate method: statsmodels ExponentialSmoothing (Holt-Winters) fit per taxonomy series, with trend and monthly (12-period) seasonality where history supports it; this is the simplest method that can capture the trend and annual seasonality the decision needs and can beat the baseline. The baseline Inspire fits is the seasonal naive forecast (the value 12 months earlier). Acceptance in plain words: a rolling-origin backtest with at least 3 folds must give MASE below 1.0 against the seasonal naive forecast; if it does not, Inspire publishes the seasonal naive forecast, flagged. Data-risk handling: seasonality is modeled with seasonal_periods = 12; missing periods are filled with 0 counts in `build_inputs` so series are continuous and the readiness gate caps missing periods at 0.2; sparse series with too little history for a seasonal fit fall back to a trend-only or non-seasonal exponential smoothing fit; forecasts are clipped at zero. No deep learning is used. Databricks AI functions are not called in these slots: Inspire's explanation and summary cells call `ai_query` on the top ranked rows to explain each trajectory and recommend the dataset build roadmap, so no additional AI call is added here.

## 6. Output Mapping

Map `entity_label` to the taxonomy value from `claims_sample_synthetic.prov_rendering_std_taxonomy` (the clinical specialty series key). `value` is the forecast monthly procedure volume, in units of distinct claims (count of `claims_sample_synthetic.claim_id`) per taxonomy per month over the forecast horizon. `segment_or_item` carries the forecast period (the target month) so each row ties a specialty to a future month. Each row's top reasons come from the series signal, not from an LLM: the direction and magnitude of the fitted trend and seasonal components plus recent observed level, which Inspire's explanation cell surfaces via `ai_query` on the top ranked rows. Set `data_quality_flag` to something other than ok when the backtest failed acceptance (MASE at or above 1.0, so the seasonal naive forecast was published instead), when a series had too few months for a seasonal fit and used the fallback, or when the series had a high share of imputed zero months. Priority tiers and recommended actions are assigned by Inspire's rule-based writer; do not ask Genie Code or an LLM to set them.

## 7. Definition of Done

- All four GENIE SLOTs are filled (`measure_readiness`, `build_inputs` with SEASON_LENGTH and HORIZON set, `forecast`, and the OUTPUT_COLUMNS / VALUE_TYPE mapping) with their function names, arguments and return columns unchanged.
- The notebook ran top to bottom in this session with run controls set to Here, then ran again as the tagged job.
- The contract-check cell (the last cell) printed PASSED.
- No Inspire cell was edited, no thresholds were changed in code, the notebook was not renamed, and no job was created or deleted; the only allowed edit outside the slots is a pinned `%pip install name==version` line if a slot needs a package the base environment lacks.
- STOP RULE: if the readiness gate raises `InspireReadinessStop` (or `InspireNoChampion` / `InspireRejected`), Genie Code must stop, show the user the plain message the gate printed, and must not lower thresholds, fabricate data, drop a check, switch tables or edit the gate to force a pass.

use_cases.Name: Estimate Patient Observation Window Length with Panel Longevity Pricing Inputs
use_cases.usecase: Quantify Cohort Longevity to Grow Revenue

## 1. Decision and Owner

This notebook changes how the Pricing Analyst sets longitudinal cohort pricing tiers by estimating how long each `hvid` stays observable in the claims stream (the observation window) and translating survival segments into panel longevity pricing inputs. The decision is owned by the Pricing Analyst and sponsored by the Chief Revenue Officer; cadence is not assessed in the DECISION BLOCK, so treat it as a periodic repricing review rather than inventing a frequency. The KPI is the count of correctly-priced panels, where better means more panels priced at a tier matching their true follow-up horizon and fewer underpriced long-horizon cohorts [ESTIMATE: depends on samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.date_service]. The ranked, per-patient observation-window output goes to the Pricing Analyst.

## 2. Data Plan

There is one table, `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic`, which serves as the event-fact table (claim-line transactions); no entity or reference table exists, so there is no join and join coverage is 1.0. The entity key is `claims_sample_synthetic.hvid`. The time column is `claims_sample_synthetic.date_service`, a STRING that must be parsed to DATE before any comparison. The as-of rule: every feature for an as-of date uses only claim rows whose parsed `date_service` is strictly before that as-of date.

Because this is survival analysis, derive per-`hvid` first and last observed service date from `claims_sample_synthetic.date_service`. The duration is the number of days from first `date_service` to last `date_service` for that `hvid`. The event is "last observed": a patient is treated as having experienced the event (observation ended, event = 1) when their last `date_service` falls at or before a censoring cutoff that is a trailing gap before `ctx["as_of_date"]` (no claims seen for the full OUTCOME_WINDOW_DAYS up to the as-of date), and is treated as censored (event = 0, still observable) when their last claim is within OUTCOME_WINDOW_DAYS of the as-of date. For scoring, return only patients whose window is still open (censored, event = 0) as of `ctx["as_of_date"]`. Population filters: keep rows with a non-null, parseable `date_service` and a non-null `hvid`. Segment features use `claims_sample_synthetic.patient_state` and a condition group derived from `claims_sample_synthetic.diagnosis_code` (for example the first three characters of the diagnosis code as the condition group).

## 3. Readiness Checks

- `row_count`: count rows in `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic` with non-null `hvid` and parseable `date_service` as of `ctx["as_of_date"]`; must be >= 1.
- `join_coverage`: single table, no join path, so set to 1.0 (meets >= 0.8).
- `outcome_derivable`: True when `date_service` parses to DATE and at least some `hvid` values have both a min and max `date_service` so a duration can be computed; otherwise False.
- `positives`: count distinct `hvid` whose event = 1 (observation window closed, last `date_service` at or before the censoring cutoff) as of `ctx["as_of_date"]`; must be >= 200.
- `class_rate`: positives (event = 1 patients) divided by total distinct `hvid`; must be between 0.005 and 0.95.
- `outcome_windows`: count the number of distinct closed trailing windows available from the `date_service` range (number of as-of windows for which a full OUTCOME_WINDOW_DAYS gap can be measured); must be >= 2.

## 4. Slot Tasks

**measure_readiness(ctx)** reads only `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic`. Parse `date_service` to DATE, filter to non-null `hvid` and parseable dates, aggregate per `hvid` to get min and max `date_service`, then compute each of the six keys exactly as in Section 3. Return the dict with keys `row_count`, `join_coverage`, `outcome_derivable`, `positives`, `class_rate`, `outcome_windows`.

**build_inputs(ctx, as_of_dates, scoring=False)** reads `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic`. Set `OUTCOME_WINDOW_DAYS` to the trailing no-claim gap that marks the end of observation (choose 180 days, since claims gaps of roughly six months indicate a patient has dropped out of the stream; this is a window-length default, not a fabricated metric). For each `hvid` and each as-of date, use only rows with parsed `date_service` strictly before the as-of date (leakage guard) to compute numeric features: tenure-to-date in days (first `date_service` to the latest `date_service` before as-of), claim count, distinct claim count, distinct `diagnosis_code` count, days since last claim before the as-of date, and one-hot or frequency encodings of `patient_state` and the condition group (first three characters of `diagnosis_code`). Return columns: `entity_id` (= `hvid`), `as_of_date` (DATE), the numeric feature columns, and optionally `entity_label` (a short string combining `patient_state` and condition group). With `scoring=True` return only `hvid` whose observation window is still open on `ctx["as_of_date"]`.

**build_label(ctx, as_of_dates)** reads the same table. For survival analysis return `entity_id`, `as_of_date`, `duration` (days from first `date_service` to last `date_service` observed up to the as-of date, floored at 0), and `event` (1 when the last `date_service` is at or before the OUTCOME_WINDOW_DAYS censoring cutoff relative to the as-of date, else 0). Use the exact rule:

```python
# per hvid, per as_of_date, over rows with date_service < as_of_date
duration = datediff(last_service, first_service)
event = 1 if datediff(as_of_date, last_service) >= OUTCOME_WINDOW_DAYS else 0
```

**fit_candidates(ctx, X_train, y_train)** sets `BASELINE_FEATURES` to the strongest signals (tenure-to-date, claim count, days since last claim). Fit at most two candidates with scikit-learn: a `GradientBoostingClassifier` (or `RandomForestClassifier`) predicting the within-window event as the risk score, with `class_weight='balanced'` where supported to handle imbalance. If the user approves a pinned survival library, a Cox model (`lifelines`) is allowed via a single pinned `%pip install lifelines==<version>` line; otherwise stay with the scikit-learn classifier. Return `{name: fitted_estimator}`.

**predict(ctx, model, X)** returns one risk score per row (probability the observation window closes within OUTCOME_WINDOW_DAYS); higher score means shorter expected observability.

**explanation_inputs(ctx, model, X)** return None to use Inspire's rule-based reasons.

## 5. Method and Baseline

The candidate method is a scikit-learn `GradientBoostingClassifier` (or `RandomForestClassifier`) that scores the probability the observation window closes within OUTCOME_WINDOW_DAYS, used as the survival risk score; Kaplan-Meier curves segmented by `patient_state` and condition group describe the segments for the explanation. The baseline Inspire fits is a balanced logistic regression on the strongest signals (`BASELINE_FEATURES`). Acceptance: on the most recent closed window (time-aware split) the model must reach a concordance index of at least 0.6 and, where measured as a classifier, out-of-time AUC of at least 0.6, PR-AUC of at least 1.5 times the class rate, and at least 0.02 AUC above the baseline. Risks: handle class imbalance with balanced weighting; address missing or sparse periods by requiring parseable `date_service` and floored durations; mitigate sparse entities by including claim-count features; seasonality is handled by the trailing-gap censoring definition. The AI step uses `ai_query` on the top output rows (called by Inspire's explanation and summary cells, not added in the slots) to explain retention segments and draft panel longevity pricing inputs; expect a short free-text response, no additional AI calls in the slots.

## 6. Output Mapping

Map `entity_label` to the `entity_label` column built in `build_inputs` (combining `patient_state` and condition group). `VALUE_TYPE` is 'risk score', so `value` is the per-`hvid` probability that the observation window closes within OUTCOME_WINDOW_DAYS (higher = shorter observability, dimensionless 0 to 1). `segment_or_item` carries the segment, the combination of `patient_state` and the condition group derived from `diagnosis_code`. Each row's top reasons come from Inspire's rule-based reasons (the most unusual feature values, since `explanation_inputs` returns None). Set `data_quality_flag` to something other than ok when `date_service` could not be parsed, when `patient_state` or `diagnosis_code` is null for the segment, or when an `hvid` has only a single claim (duration = 0, window not meaningfully estimable). Priority tiers and recommended actions are assigned by Inspire's writer; do not set them in slot code or via the LLM.

## 7. Definition of Done

- All five GENIE SLOT functions (`measure_readiness`, `build_inputs`, `build_label`, `fit_candidates`, `predict`, plus `explanation_inputs` returning None) are filled and return the exact columns named above.
- `OUTCOME_WINDOW_DAYS`, `BASELINE_FEATURES`, `OUTPUT_COLUMNS` and `VALUE_TYPE` are set.
- The notebook ran top to bottom in this session with run controls set to Here, then ran as the tagged job.

There is one table in scope, `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic`, which serves as the event facts, entity source and reference all at once; no joins are performed, so join coverage is 1.0 by definition. The entity key is `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.hvid` (one output row per patient). The time column is `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.date_service`, which is STRING, so cast it to a date for comparison. This is an unsupervised clustering use case, so there is no outcome rule to define; instead apply the as-of rule: every per-patient feature uses only claim lines whose `date_service` cast to date is strictly before `ctx["as_of_date"]`. Population filters: keep rows where `hvid` is non-null and `date_service` parses to a valid date on or before the as-of boundary; rows with unparseable `date_service` are excluded from feature windows.

- `row_count`: count claim-line rows in `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic` where `hvid` is non-null and `date_service` cast to date is strictly before `ctx["as_of_date"]`.

- `entities`: count distinct `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.hvid` over the same filtered rows (these are the patients that will be clustered).

**measure_readiness(ctx)** reads only `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic`. Apply the as-of filter on `date_service` and the non-null `hvid` filter, then return the dict with `row_count`, `join_coverage` (1.0), `entities` (distinct `hvid`), `k` (candidate segment count as described above), and `numeric_features` (count of computable numeric features). No invented numbers; all values come from the data.

**build_inputs(ctx, as_of_date)** reads only `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic`. Filter to rows with non-null `hvid` and `date_service` cast to date strictly before `as_of_date` (this is the leakage guard: no claim line on or after the as-of date contributes to any feature). Group by `hvid` and compute the numeric behaviour features: distinct count of `diagnosis_code`, distinct count of `procedure_code`, sum of `line_allowed` cast to double (treat non-numeric strings as null before summing), total claim-line frequency (row count per `hvid`), and the share of lines where `claim_type` = 'P' (professional) versus 'I' (institutional) as the claim-type mix. Return a Spark DataFrame with one row per entity: `entity_id` (the `hvid`), the numeric feature columns, and an optional `entity_label` text column (for example a short string summarizing the dominant `claim_type` and procedure diversity). Keep at least three numeric features so the readiness gate can pass.

**fit_candidates(ctx, X, seed)** builds a scikit-learn Pipeline per candidate k (impute with median, standardize with StandardScaler, then KMeans with `random_state=seed`), returning a dict like `{"kmeans_k3": pipeline, ...}` across a small range of k. No deep learning. Choose candidate k values so that entities >= 10 x k holds for the data readiness returned above.

**predict(ctx, model, X)** returns `model.predict(X)`, one integer segment number per row of X, aligned to X's row order.

**explanation_inputs(ctx, model, X)** returns None to use Inspire's rule-based reasons.

The candidate method is K-Means inside a scikit-learn Pipeline (median imputation plus StandardScaler), fit at a few candidate values of k and selected by silhouette; this is the simplest assignable clustering that keeps segment IDs stable between runs, which Score mode requires. No seasonality adjustment is needed because features are cumulative-as-of counts, not time series. No AI function is called in these slots; Inspire's explanation and summary cells call `ai_query` on the top rows only.

Map `entity_label` to the `entity_label` text column produced by `build_inputs` (the short per-patient utilization summary). use_cases.genie_instruction:
## 1. Decision and Owner

This notebook changes which condition-based cohort products the Commercial Data Product Manager designs and packages, by revealing dense clinical pathway clusters of co-occurring `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.diagnosis_code` and `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.procedure_code` values. The decision owner is the Commercial Data Product Manager and the sponsor is the Chief Commercial Officer; cadence is a single run that recomputes findings every run (DECISION BLOCK: cadence not assessed, so follow the family F single-run pattern). The KPI is packageable cohort products measured by linked diagnosis-procedure pairs per community, where more significant, high-effect-size communities counts as better [ESTIMATE: depends on `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.diagnosis_code`]. The ranked output of communities and their recommended cohort packaging goes to the Commercial Data Product Manager.

## 2. Data Plan

There is one table, `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic`, serving as event facts (claim service lines), entity, and reference all at once; there is no join, so join coverage is 1.0 by construction and no foreign key path applies. The entity key is `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.hvid` (the patient), and the time column is `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.date_service`, which is a STRING and must be cast with `to_date` before any comparison. The as-of rule: read only rows where `to_date(date_service)` is strictly before `ctx["as_of_date"]`, so no claim on or after the as-of date enters the graph. This is an unsupervised network-analysis use case (DECISION BLOCK outcome definition not assessed), so there is no outcome event or label; the findings are co-occurrence communities, not predictions. Population filters: keep only rows where both `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.diagnosis_code` and `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic.procedure_code` are non-null and non-empty after trimming, since an edge requires both endpoints.

## 3. Data Readiness Checks

- `row_count`: in `measure_readiness`, count rows of `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic` where `to_date(date_service)` is strictly before `ctx["as_of_date"]` and both `diagnosis_code` and `procedure_code` are non-null and non-empty; this is the usable edge-candidate population and must be >= 1.
- `join_coverage`: return 1.0, because this use case reads a single table and no join path exists.
- `smallest_group_rows`: group the as-of-filtered rows by the directed co-occurrence pair (`diagnosis_code`, `procedure_code`) co-occurring within the same `hvid`, count rows per pair, and return the minimum count across pairs that will become graph edges; must be >= 30 so each reported edge rests on enough observations.
- `periods`: count the distinct periods present by binning `to_date(date_service)` to year-month (`date_format(to_date(date_service), 'yyyy-MM')`) over the as-of-filtered rows and returning the distinct count; must be >= 2 so effect sizes can be computed against a prior period.

## 4. Slot Tasks

**measure_readiness(ctx)** reads only `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic`. Apply the as-of filter on `to_date(date_service)` and the non-null diagnosis/procedure filter, then compute the four keys described in Section 3 and return the dict `{'row_count', 'join_coverage', 'smallest_group_rows', 'periods'}`. Do not change thresholds; just measure.

**build_inputs(ctx)** reads only `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic` and returns a Spark DataFrame of the rows the analysis needs: select `hvid`, trimmed `diagnosis_code`, trimmed `procedure_code`, and `to_date(date_service)` as a date plus its `yyyy-MM` period label. Apply the leakage guard here: keep only rows where `to_date(date_service)` is strictly less than `ctx["as_of_date"]` (never `<=`), and drop rows with null or empty diagnosis or procedure codes. Return one row per qualifying claim service line.

**analyze(ctx, inputs)** takes that Spark DataFrame and builds the weighted co-occurrence graph: within each `hvid`, form undirected edges between each `diagnosis_code` node and each `procedure_code` co-occurring for that patient (optionally ordered by `date_service`), aggregate edge weights as co-occurrence counts across patients, then build a sparse adjacency with `scipy.sparse`, find clinical-pathway communities with `scipy.sparse.csgraph.connected_components`, and compute node centrality with a numpy power-iteration PageRank and node degree. For each community (the finding), compute an effect size as the current-period co-occurrence density or centrality versus the prior-period (or overall) baseline, a `p_value` for that difference, and `n` as the rows behind the finding. Return a pandas DataFrame with columns `entity_id` (the community id), `segment_or_item` (a representative diagnosis-procedure pair or label for the community), `value` (the effect size against the baseline), `p_value`, and `n`. Inspire applies the Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Do GraphFrames-style work with scipy and numpy only; no JAR graph libraries, no deep learning.

**OUTPUT_COLUMNS / VALUE_TYPE** is a mapping-only slot: set `entity_label` to the community label and keep `VALUE_TYPE = 'effect size'`.

## 5. Method and Baseline

The candidate method is Network Analysis built with scipy and numpy: a weighted diagnosis-procedure co-occurrence graph, communities from `scipy.sparse.csgraph.connected_components`, and influence from a numpy power-iteration PageRank. The baseline Inspire compares against is degree alone, so each community's reported effect size must show it carries structure beyond raw node degree. Acceptance rule in plain words: every reported community or influence finding must carry an effect size and must stay significant after the Benjamini-Hochberg correction at fdr_alpha = 0.05; findings that do not clear corrected significance are not accepted. Data risks: sparse entities and rare pairs are handled by the `smallest_group_rows >= 30` gate and by weighting edges with co-occurrence counts; missing periods are handled by the `periods >= 2` gate; the STRING `date_service` is cast with `to_date` and bad or null dates drop out at the filter; no values are imputed and no random stand-ins are used. No new AI function calls are added in the slots; Inspire's explanation and summary cells already call `ai_query` on the top rows to interpret each community and suggest condition-based cohort packaging.

## 6. Output Mapping

Map `entity_label` to the community label (the clinical-pathway cluster, labeled by its representative diagnosis-procedure pair). `value` is the effect size of that community's co-occurrence structure against the prior-period or overall baseline, unit: a standardized effect size (dimensionless), and `VALUE_TYPE` stays `'effect size'`. `segment_or_item` holds the group or dimension, here the representative `diagnosis_code`-`procedure_code` pair (or small set of pairs) that defines the community. Each row's top reasons are rule-based and derived from the graph: the highest-weight diagnosis-procedure edges and the highest-PageRank nodes inside that community, with the degree-baseline comparison noting the lift beyond degree alone. Set `data_quality_flag` to something other than ok when a community rests on a pair near the `smallest_group_rows` floor, when its period coverage is thin, or when a large share of its underlying rows had codes that were dropped for being empty; otherwise ok. Priority tiers and recommended actions are assigned by Inspire's writer from the corrected significance and effect size; do not have Genie Code or an LLM assign them.

## 7. Definition of Done

- All four GENIE SLOTs are filled: `measure_readiness`, `build_inputs`, `analyze`, and the `OUTPUT_COLUMNS`/`VALUE_TYPE` mapping, each keeping its function names, arguments, and return columns.
- The notebook ran top to bottom in this session with run controls set to Here, and then ran as the tagged job.
- The contract-check cell (the last cell) printed PASSED.
- No Inspire cell was edited, no thresholds were changed in code, the notebook was not renamed, and no job was created or deleted; the only allowed edit outside the slots is a pinned `%pip install name==version` line if a slot needs a package the base environment lacks.
- Only `samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic` and its real columns were cited, fully qualified, with no invented tables, columns, or numbers.
- STOP RULE: if the readiness gate raises `InspireReadinessStop` (or `InspireNoChampion` or `InspireRejected`), Genie Code must stop, show the user the plain message the gate printed, and must not lower thresholds, fabricate data, drop a check, switch tables, or edit the gate to force a pass.

use_cases.Statement: Imbalances in `patient_gender`, `patient_year_of_birth` and `patient_state` relative to clinical activity reduce how representative a cohort is, lowering its value for life-science clients requiring balanced panels.
use_cases.Solution: Databricks Genie Code engineers demographic distribution features per condition cohort and trains a classifier to label cohorts as representative or skewed, then uses ai_query to explain the imbalance and recommend sampling correction actions.
use_cases.Business Value: The Cohort Design Lead applies representativeness labels to decide which cohorts need sampling correction, increasing count of balanced sellable cohorts and reducing client-flagged demographic skew [ESTIMATE: depends on patient_year_of_birth].

Derive age from patient_year_of_birth, build per-diagnosis cohort distributions across gender, age band and state, engineer skew features (deviation from expected distribution), train a Random Forest to label representative vs skewed, then ai_query explains imbalances and drafts sampling correction actions.
use_cases.Justification: Representativeness labels guide which cohorts need sampling correction, increasing balanced sellable cohorts and reducing client-flagged skew, tied to revenue one step removed.
use_cases.Quality Summary: Signal from `patient_gender`, `patient_year_of_birth` (derive age band) and `patient_state` relative to `diagnosis_code` cohorts per `hvid`: engineer skew features (deviation from expected distribution), train a Random Forest to label cohorts representative vs skewed as a representativeness_class. ai_query explains imbalances and drafts sampling correction actions, raising balanced sellable cohorts [ESTIMATE: depends on patient_year_of_birth].
use_cases.bob_justification: `patient_gender`, `patient_year_of_birth`, `patient_state` give skew features but 'expected distribution' needs an unstated reference; weakest D19 (correction impact unprovable).

domains.summary:
The Quality domain safeguards the trust that underpins every Samples healthverity data product. By ensuring claims are accurate, complete, and free of duplication, this domain protects both revenue and the organization's reputation as a reliable data partner.

Its impact is direct and measurable. Detect Billing Anomalies to Prevent Revenue Loss gives the Data Quality Lead a ranked provider investigation queue, increasing the share of flagged anomalies caught early. Classify Coding Completeness to Improve Data Quality lets the Data Curation Lead work a pre-release correction list to raise the share of fully-coded claims. Prevent Duplicate Billing to Protect Revenue provides a weekly review queue of suspected duplicate clusters to lift the share of de-duplicated records.

With Databricks Genie Code, quality teams can triage, investigate, and validate data issues conversationally, turning data integrity from a cost center into a competitive differentiator for Samples healthverity.

use_cases.Name: Detect Abnormal Provider Billing Patterns with Investigation Queue
use_cases.usecase: Detect Billing Anomalies to Prevent Revenue Loss
use_cases.Statement: Unusual billing behavior by rendering providers, visible across `prov_rendering_npi`, `line_charge`, and `procedure_units_billed`, can indicate upcoding or billing errors that distort real-world evidence quality and erode data trust with licensing clients.
use_cases.Solution: Databricks Genie Code engineers per-provider billing features and trains an Isolation Forest to flag providers whose charge and unit patterns deviate from peers, producing a ranked investigation queue.
use_cases.Business Value: The Data Quality Lead receives a ranked provider investigation queue, increasing the share of flagged anomalies in `line_charge` and `procedure_units_billed` reviewed before data release and preventing distorted claims from reaching clients [ESTIMATE: depends on `line_charge`].
use_cases.High Level Design: Using columns: prov_rendering_npi, line_charge, procedure_units_billed, procedure_code, claim_type. Approach: cast line_charge and procedure_units_billed to numeric, aggregate per prov_rendering_npi (mean charge, charge-per-unit, procedure diversity, claim_type mix), train an Isolation Forest (contamination=0.05) on these features, rank providers by anomaly score, then use ai_query to explain each flagged provider and recommend investigation steps.
use_cases.Justification: Flagging abnormal billing protects RWD quality and data trust, mitigating a risk KPI; money effect is indirect via client trust and retention.
use_cases.Quality Summary: Signal from numeric-cast `line_charge` and `procedure_units_billed`, plus `procedure_code` and `claim_type` aggregated per `prov_rendering_npi` into mean charge, charge-per-unit and procedure diversity features. An Isolation Forest (contamination=0.05) scores providers, producing a billing_anomaly_score ranked queue. ai_query explains each flag, delivering a pre-release investigation queue [ESTIMATE: depends on line_charge].
use_cases.bob_justification: `prov_rendering_npi`, `line_charge`, `procedure_units_billed` give per-provider billing features for Isolation Forest; weakest D8 (overlaps other anomaly UCs).

use_cases.technique_implementation_guidance:
Method: Isolation Forest, or Local Outlier Factor with novelty=True, from scikit-learn on numeric signals, fitted on a reference window that always precedes the scored window.

Accept: the alerts fit the review budget, the top alerts of two fits with different seeds agree at the stability threshold, and precision on any known cases is not below the baseline.
If data is insufficient: too few reference rows or mostly missing key signals stop the run at the readiness gate; never score with a detector trained on a thin window.

use_cases.Solution: Databricks Genie Code engineers per-claim fingerprints from the billing fields, trains an Isolation Forest to flag statistically unusual duplicate clusters, then calls ai_query to explain each flagged cluster and draft a billing integrity review entry.
use_cases.Business Value: The Data Quality Lead works a weekly review queue of suspected duplicate clusters, increasing the share of de-duplicated claims and reducing erroneous `line_charge` totals carried into licensed datasets [ESTIMATE: depends on `line_charge`].

use_cases.Solution: Databricks Genie Code models expected allowed amounts as a function of charge, procedure, and setting, flags claims whose actual allowed amounts deviate sharply from the model, and produces a pricing review queue.

Baseline: a robust z-score rule (median and MAD) on the same signals.
Accept: the alerts fit the review budget, the top alerts of two fits with different seeds agree at the stability threshold, and precision on any known cases is not below the baseline.
If data is insufficient: too few reference rows or mostly missing key signals stop the run at the readiness gate; never score with a detector trained on a thin window.

use_cases.Name: Predict Patient Longitudinal Continuity with Data Gap Remediation Actions
use_cases.usecase: Predict Record Continuity to Improve Data Quality
use_cases.Statement: Longitudinal patient journeys depend on continuous claim activity per `hvid` over `date_service`, but patients who stop appearing create gaps that weaken the dataset's value for life-sciences research, and these drop-offs are not predicted in advance.
use_cases.Solution: Databricks Genie Code models time-to-last-observation per patient using survival analysis to estimate continuity risk, producing a list of patients likely to drop from the longitudinal record for data gap remediation.
use_cases.Business Value: The Clinical Data Scientist targets at-risk longitudinal records for enrichment, increasing retained continuous patient journeys measured by active `hvid` spans over `date_service` and improving dataset research value [ESTIMATE: depends on `hvid`].
use_cases.High Level Design: Using columns: hvid, date_service, claim_id, diagnosis_code. Approach: per hvid compute observation start, last claim date and inter-claim gaps from date_service, define the event as prolonged absence of new claim_id, fit a Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional-hazards model using claim frequency and diagnosis diversity as covariates, then use ai_query to explain drop-off risk and recommend data gap remediation actions.
use_cases.Justification: Predicting longitudinal drop-off helps preserve continuous patient journeys that drive research value and dataset price; revenue link one step removed.
use_cases.Quality Summary: Signal from `hvid` and `date_service` yields per-patient observation start, last claim date and inter-claim gaps; event is prolonged absence of new `claim_id`. Kaplan-Meier and Cox PH models with claim frequency and `diagnosis_code` diversity covariates estimate a continuity_risk hazard per patient. ai_query drafts remediation actions, targeting at-risk journeys to retain continuous spans [ESTIMATE: depends on hvid].
use_cases.bob_justification: `hvid` over `date_service` supports survival analysis of continuity but 'drop-off' is censoring, not true attrition; weakest D16 (remediation action is vague).
use_cases.available_tables_listing: Only the primary tables are available: samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic
use_cases.technique_implementation_guidance:
Method: time-to-event with censoring: a risk score from a scikit-learn classifier of the event within the window, or a Cox model if the user approves installing a pinned survival library; describe groups with Kaplan-Meier curves.
Baseline: a balanced logistic regression on the strongest signals.
Accept: the concordance index on the most recent closed window meets the threshold and beats the baseline by the minimum gain (time-aware split).
If data is insufficient: too few events or fewer than two closed windows stop the run at the readiness gate.

use_cases.Name: Reveal Procedure Modifier Overuse with Coding Review Prioritization
use_cases.usecase: Flag Modifier Misuse to Ensure Compliance
use_cases.Statement: A small set of providers may concentrate disproportionate use of procedure modifiers (`procedure_modifier_1` through `procedure_modifier_4`), a pattern associated with coding irregularities that reduce the trustworthiness of claims data.
use_cases.Solution: Databricks Genie Code computes modifier-usage rates per provider, applies Pareto concentration analysis to isolate the top contributors to modifier volume, then uses ai_query to explain outlier providers and draft a coding review prioritization list.
use_cases.Business Value: The Compliance Analyst prioritizes coding reviews on providers concentrating modifier use, increasing count of reviewed high-modifier providers and reducing modifier-related data-quality complaints [ESTIMATE: depends on procedure_modifier_1].
use_cases.High Level Design: Using columns: prov_billing_npi, procedure_modifier_1, procedure_modifier_2, procedure_modifier_3, procedure_modifier_4, claim_id. Compute per-provider modifier-presence rate across the four modifier fields, run Pareto analysis to find the top contributors driving modifier volume, then ai_query explains outlier providers and drafts a coding review prioritization list.
use_cases.Justification: Prioritizing coding reviews on modifier-overuse providers reduces data-quality complaints, a quality KPI with indirect money effect.
use_cases.Quality Summary: Signal from `procedure_modifier_1` through `procedure_modifier_4` presence per `prov_billing_npi` across `claim_id` volume: compute a per-provider modifier_presence_rate, apply Pareto to isolate the top contributors to modifier volume. ai_query explains outlier providers and drafts a coding review prioritization list, reducing modifier-related data-quality complaints [ESTIMATE: depends on procedure_modifier_1].
use_cases.bob_justification: `procedure_modifier_1` through `_4` by `prov_billing_npi` support modifier-rate Pareto but overuse is a weak proxy for irregularity; weakest D9 (shallow concentration logic).

domains.summary:
The Partnerships domain determines the breadth and depth of Samples healthverity's data footprint, directing sourcing toward the specialties, hubs, and providers that most expand coverage and value. Strong partnerships translate directly into richer cohorts and more complete offerings.

The opportunities are strategic. Fill Specialty Coverage Gaps to Grow Revenue allows the Data Acquisition Manager to prioritize which specialty data to source next, increasing complete specialty cohorts. Prioritize Referral Hubs to Grow Revenue helps the Partnerships Lead target outreach to high-centrality provider hubs, while Prioritize Provider Networks to Grow Revenue focuses sourcing on top-contributing providers to raise high-value claim coverage.

Databricks Genie Code lets partnership teams interrogate network centrality, coverage gaps, and provider contribution in plain language, sharpening outreach decisions and accelerating the growth of Samples healthverity's data supply.

use_cases.Name: Predict Provider Taxonomy Specialty Gaps with Sourcing Prioritization List
use_cases.usecase: Fill Specialty Coverage Gaps to Grow Revenue
use_cases.Statement: Under-represented provider specialties in `prov_rendering_std_taxonomy` relative to the diagnosis and procedure mix they treat create coverage gaps that reduce the completeness of licensed specialty cohorts.
use_cases.Solution: Databricks Genie Code clusters providers by their taxonomy and clinical activity profile using K-Means, identifies sparse specialty clusters against the diagnosis-procedure demand, then calls ai_query to explain gaps and draft a data sourcing prioritization list.
use_cases.Business Value: The Data Acquisition Manager prioritizes which specialty data to source next, increasing count of complete specialty cohorts and reducing coverage gaps flagged by clients [ESTIMATE: depends on prov_rendering_std_taxonomy].
use_cases.High Level Design: Using columns: prov_rendering_std_taxonomy, diagnosis_code, procedure_code, prov_rendering_npi, claim_id. Build per-provider feature vectors (taxonomy, distinct diagnosis_code count, distinct procedure_code count, claim volume), run K-Means clustering to find sparse specialty clusters, then ai_query explains the gaps and drafts a sourcing prioritization list.
use_cases.Justification: Identifying under-represented specialty cohorts guides which data to source next, enabling more complete sellable cohorts; revenue impact is one step removed via future licensing.
use_cases.Quality Summary: Signal from `prov_rendering_std_taxonomy` (specialty), distinct `diagnosis_code` and `procedure_code` counts and `claim_id` volume per `prov_rendering_npi` build per-provider feature vectors. K-Means clustering groups specialties and identifies sparse clusters against clinical demand, producing a specialty_coverage_gap metric. ai_query drafts a sourcing prioritization list, delivering completeness gains [ESTIMATE: depends on prov_rendering_std_taxonomy].
use_cases.bob_justification: `prov_rendering_std_taxonomy`, `diagnosis_code`, `procedure_code` cluster providers but 'specialty gap' is a derived judgment; weakest D17 (sparse-cluster logic is subjective).
use_cases.available_tables_listing: Only the primary tables are available: samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic
use_cases.technique_implementation_guidance:
Method: K-Means or a Gaussian mixture inside a scikit-learn Pipeline with imputation and scaling, choosing the number of segments by silhouette. Use only models that can assign new entities, so segment IDs stay stable between runs.
Baseline: quantile tiers on the most variable feature.
Accept: silhouette, the smallest segment share and bootstrap stability (adjusted Rand index) meet the thresholds.
If data is insufficient: too few entities for the number of segments or fewer than three usable numeric features stop the run at the readiness gate.

use_cases.Name: Reveal Referral Network Hubs with Provider Partnership Targeting
use_cases.usecase: Prioritize Referral Hubs to Grow Revenue
use_cases.Statement: Referral relationships between `prov_referring_npi` and `prov_rendering_npi` form a provider network whose influential hubs indicate where data-partnership outreach yields the broadest patient coverage.
use_cases.Solution: Databricks Genie Code constructs a referral graph from the referring and rendering NPI edges, computes PageRank and betweenness centrality with GraphFrames, then uses ai_query to profile top hubs and draft a partnership targeting list.
use_cases.Business Value: The Partnerships Lead targets outreach to high-centrality provider hubs, increasing count of high-coverage partnerships and reducing wasted outreach to low-connectivity providers [ESTIMATE: depends on prov_referring_npi].
use_cases.High Level Design: Using columns: prov_referring_npi, prov_rendering_npi, hvid, claim_id. Build a directed edge list from prov_referring_npi to prov_rendering_npi weighted by distinct hvid count, run PageRank and betweenness centrality via GraphFrames to rank hub providers, then ai_query profiles each hub and drafts a partnership targeting list.
use_cases.Justification: Referral-graph centrality identifies high-coverage partnership hubs, informing sourcing outreach that expands patient coverage; revenue link is one step removed through downstream licensing.
use_cases.Quality Summary: Signal from `prov_referring_npi` to `prov_rendering_npi` forms directed edges, weighted by distinct `hvid` count to measure patient coverage per referral. GraphFrames PageRank and betweenness centrality rank hub providers, producing a hub_centrality score per NPI. ai_query profiles top hubs into a targeting list, delivering coverage-maximizing partnership outreach [ESTIMATE: depends on prov_referring_npi].
use_cases.bob_justification: `prov_referring_npi` to `prov_rendering_npi` edges weighted by `hvid` form a valid referral graph; weakest D19 (partnership impact hard to attribute from synthetic data).

use_cases.technique_implementation_guidance:
Method: build the graph from the relationship columns, then compute degree, connected components (scipy.sparse.csgraph) and a power-iteration PageRank with numpy; JAR-based graph libraries cannot load on serverless notebooks.
Baseline: degree alone.
Accept: every reported influence or community finding carries an effect size and a Benjamini-Hochberg corrected significance.
If data is insufficient: nodes below the minimum rows or fewer than two periods stop the run at the readiness gate.

use_cases.Name: Prioritize High-Value Provider Networks with Data Partnership Targeting
use_cases.usecase: Prioritize Provider Networks to Grow Revenue
use_cases.Statement: Claim volume and charges concentrate among a subset of billing providers captured in `prov_billing_npi`, `claim_id`, and `line_charge`, but without quantifying this concentration the partnership team cannot focus data-sourcing efforts on the providers contributing the richest claim data.
use_cases.Solution: Databricks Genie Code ranks billing providers by claim volume and charge contribution, applies Pareto analysis to isolate the vital few driving most data value, and produces a partnership target list.
use_cases.Business Value: The Data Partnerships Manager focuses sourcing outreach on top-contributing providers, increasing high-value claim coverage measured by `claim_id` volume and `line_charge` share per `prov_billing_npi` [ESTIMATE: depends on `line_charge`].
use_cases.High Level Design: Using columns: prov_billing_npi, claim_id, line_charge, prov_billing_std_taxonomy. Approach: aggregate distinct claim_id counts and numeric-cast line_charge sums per prov_billing_npi, rank providers and compute cumulative contribution to apply the 80/20 Pareto rule, enrich with prov_billing_std_taxonomy, then use ai_query to explain the vital-few providers and recommend partnership targeting.
use_cases.Justification: Targeting the vital-few providers that contribute richest claim data directly supports data-sourcing to expand licensable coverage, a recurring commercial decision tied to revenue expansion.
use_cases.Quality Summary: Signal from `prov_billing_npi` (provider grain), `claim_id` (volume) and numeric-cast `line_charge` (value): aggregate distinct claim_id counts and summed line_charge per provider, rank and compute cumulative contribution for an 80/20 Pareto split, enrich with `prov_billing_std_taxonomy`. Produces a provider_contribution_share KPI and a vital-few target list, delivering partnership targeting [ESTIMATE: depends on line_charge].
use_cases.bob_justification: `prov_billing_npi`, `claim_id`, `line_charge` enable Pareto ranking but `line_charge` is STRING needing cast; weakest D9 (80/20 is shallow analytically).

use_cases.Name: Forecast Monthly Claim Volume with Capacity Planning Recommendations
use_cases.usecase: Forecast Claim Volume to Reduce Operational Cost
use_cases.Statement: Claim submission volume fluctuates over time across the dataset captured in `date_service` and `claim_id`, making it hard for data operations teams to plan ingestion and curation capacity, risking backlog and delayed data delivery to licensing clients.
use_cases.Solution: Databricks Genie Code aggregates distinct `claim_id` counts by month derived from `date_service`, fits a time-series forecast, and projects future claim volume so the operations team can pre-allocate processing capacity.
use_cases.Business Value: The Data Operations Manager uses the monthly claim-volume projection to schedule ingestion capacity ahead of demand, reducing processing backlog measured by claim counts per period from `claim_id` and improving on-time data delivery [ESTIMATE: depends on `claim_id`].
use_cases.High Level Design: Using columns: claim_id, date_service. Approach: parse date_service into a monthly period, aggregate distinct claim_id counts per month to build a time series, fit Prophet or ai_forecast with calendar seasonality features, then use ai_query to explain the projected trajectory and recommend capacity scheduling actions.
use_cases.Justification: Operational capacity planning improves on-time data delivery but its revenue link is indirect; on synthetic sample data the forecast is illustrative, not a direct revenue mover.
use_cases.Quality Summary: Signal from `date_service` (temporal) and `claim_id` (volume) supports a monthly time series: parse date_service to month, count distinct claim_id per period to produce a claims_per_month KPI, then fit Prophet/ai_forecast with seasonality to project future volume. The projection feeds ingestion capacity scheduling, delivering the capacity planning outcome [ESTIMATE: depends on claim_id].
use_cases.bob_justification: `date_service` and `claim_id` support monthly volume forecasting but `date_service` is STRING needing parsing; weakest D15 (synthetic sample has no live refresh for capacity decisions).
use_cases.available_tables_listing: Only the primary tables are available: samples.healthverity.claims_sample_synthetic
use_cases.technique_implementation_guidance:
Method: refit on the full history every run (statsmodels exponential smoothing or SARIMAX per series, or one gradient-boosted model with calendar and lag features across series); never register per-series models. ai_forecast() runs only through a SQL warehouse, not in this notebook.
Baseline: the seasonal naive forecast (the value one season earlier).
Accept: a rolling-origin backtest with at least three folds gives MASE below 1 against the seasonal naive forecast; otherwise the notebook publishes the seasonal naive forecast, flagged.
If data is insufficient: fewer than two seasonal cycles, stale data or many missing periods stop the run at the readiness gate.
